questions.q: What colors are on the American flag?
questions.explain: The American flag is red, white and blue.
questions.tip: Red, white and blue, just like a firework's boom: red, white, BLUE!

questions.q: What shapes are in the blue part of the American flag?
questions.explain: The blue part of the flag is full of white stars.
questions.tip: Look up at night: stars live in the dark blue sky, and on the flag too!

questions.q: The American flag has long red and white lines. What are they called?
questions.explain: The red and white lines on the flag are called stripes.
questions.tip: Stripes are like a candy cane: red, white, red, white!

questions.q: The American flag is the flag of which country?
questions.explain: The red, white and blue flag with stars and stripes is the flag of the United States of America.
questions.tip: Stars and stripes, USA, we wave it high on the Fourth of July!

questions.q: When we say the Pledge of Allegiance, where do we put our right hand?
questions.explain: We put our right hand over our heart to show respect for the flag.
questions.tip: Hand on heart means I love my country with all my heart.

questions.q: What do we say to the flag at school in the morning?
questions.explain: Many schools say the Pledge of Allegiance to the flag each morning.
questions.tip: Pledge means promise: each morning we make a promise to the flag.

questions.q: True or false: The American flag has stars on it.
questions.explain: True! The flag has white stars on a blue square.
questions.tip: Twinkle, twinkle, little star, 50 on the flag, near and far!

questions.q: Which bird is a symbol of America?
questions.explain: The bald eagle is the national bird and a symbol of the United States.
questions.tip: The bald eagle soars high and free, the bird of the land of liberty!

questions.q: The Statue of Liberty is a big statue of a lady. What does she hold up high in her hand?
questions.explain: The Statue of Liberty holds a torch up high. Its light stands for freedom.
questions.tip: Lady Liberty lights the way with her torch held high.

questions.q: The Liberty Bell is a famous old bell. What does it have?
questions.explain: The Liberty Bell has a big crack in it, so it is not rung anymore.
questions.tip: Ding, dong, CRACK! The Liberty Bell cracked and can't ring back.

questions.q: On the Fourth of July we celebrate America's birthday. What do people often watch that night?
questions.explain: The Fourth of July is Independence Day, and many people watch fireworks.
questions.tip: Happy birthday, America! Fireworks are the birthday candles in the sky.

questions.q: The national anthem is a special kind of what?
questions.explain: The national anthem is a song about our country. It is called The Star-Spangled Banner.
questions.tip: Anthem rhymes with... well, nothing, but you SING it!

questions.q: True or false: The Statue of Liberty is green.
questions.explain: True! The statue is made of copper, which slowly turned green over many years.
questions.tip: Copper turns green like an old penny left out in the rain.

questions.q: Who is the leader of our whole country?
questions.explain: The President is the leader of the United States.
questions.tip: The President is like the captain of America's team.

questions.q: Where does the President live?
questions.explain: The President lives and works in the White House.
questions.tip: The White House is the President's house, painted all white.

questions.q: What color is the White House?
questions.explain: Just like its name, the White House is white.
questions.tip: The answer is right in the name: WHITE House!

questions.q: How do grown-ups pick the President?
choices: They pick a name from a hat
questions.explain: Grown-up citizens vote to choose the President.
questions.tip: Vote, vote, pick the boat: grown-ups vote to choose who leads.

questions.q: True or false: The President lives in the White House.
questions.explain: True! The White House is the home of the President.
questions.tip: President plus White House, a perfect pair like peanut butter and jelly.

questions.q: The White House is in a city. Which city?
questions.explain: The White House is in Washington, D.C., the capital of the United States.
questions.tip: D.C. is where the President you'll see.

questions.q: Your friend wants a turn on the swing. What is a good thing to do?
questions.explain: Taking turns is fair and kind. Good citizens share.
questions.tip: Taking turns makes everyone grin: you go, I go, we all win!

questions.q: Why do we have rules?
choices: To keep us safe and be fair
questions.explain: Rules help keep everyone safe and help us treat each other fairly.
questions.tip: Rules are like a seat belt: they keep us safe and sound.

questions.q: You see trash on the playground. What can you do to help?
choices: Throw it in the trash can
questions.explain: Picking up trash helps keep our community clean. That is being a good citizen.
questions.tip: See it, pick it, bin it!

questions.q: What should you do when a traffic light is red?
questions.explain: Red means stop. Following safety rules keeps people safe.
questions.tip: Red means stop, green means go, yellow means slow!

questions.q: Who helps keep us safe in our town?
questions.explain: Police officers and firefighters are community helpers who keep us safe.
questions.tip: Helpers in blue and helpers in red trucks keep our town safe.

questions.q: True or false: Being kind to others is part of being a good citizen.
questions.explain: True! Good citizens are kind, helpful and fair to others.
questions.tip: Kind is a superpower every good citizen has.

questions.q: Your teacher says, quiet time now. What should you do?
questions.explain: Following class rules helps everyone learn.
questions.tip: Zip your lips and open your ears!

questions.q: How many stars are on the American flag?
questions.explain: The flag has 50 stars, one for each state.
questions.tip: 50 stars for 50 states, one star each, like a name tag.

questions.q: How many stripes are on the American flag?
questions.explain: The flag has 13 stripes: 7 red and 6 white.
questions.tip: 13 stripes for 13 colonies, the very first states in the country's story.

questions.q: What do the 50 stars on the flag stand for?
questions.explain: Each star stands for one of the 50 states.
questions.tip: Stars equal states: both start with ST!

questions.q: What do the 13 stripes on the flag stand for?
questions.explain: The 13 stripes stand for the 13 colonies that became the first states.
questions.tip: Stripes are for the start: the 13 colonies.

questions.q: What is a nickname for the American flag?
questions.explain: The flag is often called the Stars and Stripes or Old Glory.
questions.tip: Just say what you see: stars and stripes!

questions.q: When we say the Pledge of Allegiance, we promise to be loyal to what?
questions.explain: The Pledge is a promise of loyalty to the flag and to the United States.
questions.tip: Pledge to the flag, pledge to the land.

questions.q: How do people usually stand for the Pledge of Allegiance?
choices: Facing the flag with the right hand over the heart
Sitting on the floor with eyes closed
questions.explain: People stand, face the flag and put their right hand over their heart.
questions.tip: Face the flag, right hand on heart, stand up tall from the start.

questions.q: What color is the square with the stars on the flag?
questions.explain: The stars sit on a blue square in the top corner of the flag.
questions.tip: Stars shine in a blue sky, so the star square is blue.

questions.q: True or false: The stripes on the flag are red and white.
questions.explain: True! The flag has red and white stripes.
questions.tip: Red and white like a peppermint stripe.

questions.q: Flag Day celebrates the American flag. In which month is Flag Day?
questions.explain: Flag Day is June 14.
questions.tip: June has a flag tune: Flag Day is June 14.

questions.q: What is the name of the national anthem?
questions.explain: The national anthem of the United States is The Star-Spangled Banner.
questions.tip: Star-Spangled Banner: the flag still waved over Fort McHenry.

questions.q: Who wrote the words to The Star-Spangled Banner?
questions.explain: Francis Scott Key wrote the words in 1814 after seeing the flag still flying over a fort.
questions.tip: Francis Scott KEY wrote the KEY song of our country.

questions.q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
questions.explain: The people of France gave the Statue of Liberty as a gift of friendship.
questions.tip: France sent a friendship present: a giant green lady!

questions.q: In which city's harbor does the Statue of Liberty stand?
questions.explain: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor.
questions.tip: Lady Liberty says hello to ships sailing into New York.

questions.q: In which city is the Liberty Bell?
questions.explain: The Liberty Bell is in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
questions.tip: Philadelphia means city of brotherly love, and the Liberty Bell lives there.

questions.q: What is the national bird of the United States?
questions.explain: The bald eagle is the national bird. It appears on the Great Seal of the United States.
questions.tip: Eagle, eagle, strong and free, America's bird it will always be.

questions.q: On what date do we celebrate Independence Day?
questions.explain: Independence Day is July 4. It celebrates the day in 1776 the Declaration of Independence was adopted.
questions.tip: Fourth of July, fireworks in the sky!

questions.q: Which character with a tall hat and white beard is a symbol of the US government?
questions.explain: Uncle Sam, often drawn in red, white and blue, is a symbol of the United States.
questions.tip: Uncle Sam has the same initials as the United States: U.S.!

questions.q: True or false: The bald eagle is bald, with no feathers on its head.
questions.explain: False! A bald eagle has white feathers on its head. Long ago, bald could mean white.
questions.tip: A bald eagle wears a white feather hat, not a bare head.

questions.q: What is the capital city of the United States?
questions.explain: Washington, D.C. is the capital, where the President and Congress work.
questions.tip: Washington, D.C. was named after George Washington, our first President.

questions.q: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.explain: George Washington was the first President.
questions.tip: George Washington is on the one-dollar bill: number one bill, number one President.

questions.q: Who leads a city?
questions.explain: A mayor is the leader of a city or town.
questions.tip: Mayor of the city, it is pretty witty.

questions.q: Who leads a state?
questions.explain: Each state has a governor as its leader.
questions.tip: Governor for a state, Mayor for a city, President for the country.

questions.q: Who leads the whole country?
questions.explain: The President is the leader of the United States.
questions.tip: President of the whole land, the leader of the band.

questions.q: How many years does a President serve in one term?
questions.explain: A President is elected for a four-year term.
questions.tip: A President's term is 4 years, just like the Olympics come every 4 years.

questions.q: What is the building called where the President lives and works?
questions.explain: The President lives and works in the White House.
questions.tip: The President's house is the White House.

questions.q: Congress makes the country's laws. In which building does Congress meet?
questions.explain: Congress meets in the US Capitol building, which has a big white dome.
questions.tip: Capitol with an O has a dome on top; Congress meets under the dome.

questions.q: True or false: A king rules the United States.
questions.explain: False! The United States has no king. The people vote for their leaders.
questions.tip: No crown in this town: Americans vote for their leaders.

questions.q: What is a law?
choices: A rule that everyone in a place must follow
questions.explain: Laws are rules made by the government that everyone must follow.
questions.tip: A law is a rule for everyone, everywhere in the land.

questions.q: Why do we wear seat belts in the car?
choices: To stay safe, and it is the law
To make the car go faster
questions.explain: Seat belts keep us safe in a crash, and laws say we must wear them.
questions.tip: Click it before you go; it's the law, you know!

questions.q: Who helps people follow the law and stay safe?
questions.explain: Police officers help enforce laws and keep communities safe.
questions.tip: Police protect: P for police, P for protect.

questions.q: Who decides what happens when people disagree about a law in court?
questions.explain: Judges work in courts and help settle disagreements about the law.
questions.tip: Judge sounds like JUDGE-ment: a judge decides.

questions.q: Where is the safest place to cross the street?
choices: In the middle of the block
questions.explain: Crosswalks are the safe place to cross. Look both ways first.
questions.tip: Stripes on the street say cross here with your feet.

questions.q: Which of these is a good citizen?
choices: Someone who follows rules and helps others
Someone who is mean to others
questions.explain: Good citizens follow rules, are honest and help their community.
questions.tip: Good citizens follow, help and share.

questions.q: True or false: Laws are the same for everyone, even leaders.
questions.explain: True! In America, everyone must follow the law, including leaders. This is called the rule of law.
questions.tip: Nobody is above the law, not even the boss.

questions.q: What happens if there were no rules at a game?
choices: It would not be fair and people might get hurt
questions.explain: Rules make games fair and safe. Laws do the same for a country.
questions.tip: No rules, no fun: just ask anyone who played tag where nobody is ever it.

questions.q: What does a stop sign tell drivers to do?
questions.explain: A red stop sign tells drivers to come to a full stop.
questions.tip: Eight sides, red and bright, S-T-O-P means stop right.

questions.q: What does it mean to vote?
questions.explain: When you vote, you make your choice known.
questions.tip: Vote equals choose: you pick, you choose!

questions.q: Your class votes on a game. 15 kids pick tag and 7 kids pick hopscotch. Which game wins?
questions.explain: Tag got more votes. In a vote, the choice with the most votes usually wins.
questions.tip: Most votes wins, just like the biggest pile wins.

questions.q: How old must a citizen be to vote for President?
questions.explain: US citizens can vote when they are 18 years old.
questions.tip: 18 to vote: you can vote when you are grown.

questions.q: What is the paper or screen people use to vote called?
questions.explain: People mark their choices on a ballot.
questions.tip: A BALLot: you mark your choice and drop it in, like a ball in a hoop.

questions.q: In an election, how many times can each person vote?
choices: As many times as they want
questions.explain: Each voter gets one vote. That keeps elections fair.
questions.tip: One person, one vote: fair for everyone.

questions.q: True or false: In America, your vote is secret.
questions.explain: True! Voters mark their ballot in private, so no one has to know how they voted.
questions.tip: Your vote is your secret, like a wish on a birthday candle.

questions.q: Why is voting important?
choices: It lets people choose their leaders
questions.explain: Voting lets citizens choose leaders and have a say in their government.
questions.tip: Voting is your voice: it lets you say who leads.

questions.q: In which month do Americans vote for President?
questions.explain: Elections for President are held in November.
questions.tip: November: vote, then Thanksgiving turkey!

questions.q: Who helps put out fires?
questions.explain: Firefighters put out fires and help people stay safe. They are community helpers.
questions.tip: Firefighters fight fires: it's right in their name!

questions.q: Who takes care of sick animals?
questions.explain: A veterinarian, or vet, is a doctor for animals.
questions.tip: A vet is a doctor for pets.

questions.q: Who brings letters and packages to your home?
questions.explain: Mail carriers deliver letters and packages.
questions.tip: Mail carriers carry the mail.

questions.q: Who helps you find books at the library?
questions.explain: A librarian takes care of the library and helps people find books.
questions.tip: Library, librarian: the helper's name hides in the place's name.

questions.q: Which one is a need, not a want?
questions.explain: Needs are things we must have to live, like water, food and a home. Wants are nice to have.
questions.tip: Need it to live? It's a need. Just nice to have? It's a want.

questions.q: Which one is a want, not a need?
questions.explain: You can live without a new toy, so it is a want. Food, water and a home are needs.
questions.tip: A want is a wish; a need is a must.

questions.q: Money you keep to use later is called...
questions.say: Money you keep to use later is called what?
questions.explain: Savings is money you put away, like in a piggy bank, to use later.
questions.tip: Save it in a piggy bank for later: that's savings.

questions.q: A farmer grows apples to sell. What is the farmer?
questions.explain: A producer makes or grows things to sell. A consumer buys and uses them.
questions.tip: Producers produce, or make; consumers consume, or use.

questions.q: You buy an apple and eat it. What are you?
questions.explain: A consumer is a person who buys and uses goods, like food.
questions.tip: Consume means use up, like eating a snack.

questions.q: Which one is a way to be a good citizen?
questions.explain: Good citizens are honest, follow the rules and treat others kindly.
questions.tip: Be honest, be kind, be fair.

questions.q: How many branches does the US government have?
questions.explain: The three branches are legislative, executive and judicial.
questions.tip: Three branches like a tree: Legislative, Executive, Judicial, L-E-J.

questions.q: Which branch makes the laws?
questions.explain: The legislative branch, Congress, makes federal laws.
questions.tip: LEgislative = LEgislate = make Laws: both have an L for Laws.

questions.q: Which branch carries out and enforces the laws?
questions.explain: The executive branch, led by the President, carries out the laws.
questions.tip: EXecutive EXecutes: it carries out the laws.

questions.q: Which branch explains the laws and decides if they follow the Constitution?
questions.explain: The judicial branch, the courts, interprets the laws.
questions.tip: JUDicial has JUDges who JUDge the laws.

questions.q: What is the name for the legislative branch of the US government?
questions.explain: Congress is the legislative branch.
questions.tip: Congress comes together: con means together, like a convention of lawmakers.

questions.q: What are the two parts of Congress?
choices: The Senate and the House of Representatives
The President and the Vice President
The Supreme Court and the Cabinet
questions.explain: Congress has two parts, or houses: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
questions.tip: Senate and House: two rooms in one big law-making home.

questions.q: Who is the head of the executive branch?
questions.explain: The President leads the executive branch.
questions.tip: The President PRESIDES over the executive branch.

questions.q: What is the highest court in the United States?
questions.explain: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the nation.
questions.tip: Supreme means the top, the best, the highest court.

questions.q: Why does the government have three branches?
choices: So no one branch becomes too powerful
So the President can make all the decisions
questions.explain: Splitting power among three branches, with checks and balances, keeps any one branch from becoming too powerful.
questions.tip: Three branches share the power, like friends sharing a pizza so no one hogs it.

questions.q: What is it called when the President rejects a bill passed by Congress?
questions.explain: The President can veto, or reject, a bill.
questions.tip: Veto is Latin for I forbid; the President says no way, veto!

questions.q: How many justices are on the Supreme Court?
questions.explain: The Supreme Court has nine justices, including the Chief Justice.
questions.tip: Nine justices, like nine players on a baseball team.

g35.name: The Constitution and Bill of Rights

questions.q: What is the supreme law of the land?
questions.explain: The Constitution is the supreme law of the United States.
questions.tip: The Constitution is the boss of all the laws.

questions.q: In which year was the Constitution written?
questions.explain: The Constitution was written at the Constitutional Convention in 1787.
questions.tip: In 1787, the Constitution came to heaven: 11 years after 1776.

questions.q: In which city was the Constitution written?
questions.explain: Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 to write the Constitution.
questions.tip: Philadelphia is America's birthplace: the Declaration AND the Constitution were written there.

questions.q: What are the first three words of the Constitution?
questions.explain: The Constitution begins with We the People, showing that the government gets its power from the people.
questions.tip: We the People: the people are in charge!

questions.q: What is an amendment?
choices: A change or addition to the Constitution
questions.explain: An amendment is a change or addition to the Constitution.
questions.tip: Amend means mend or fix: an amendment changes the Constitution.

questions.q: What do we call the first ten amendments to the Constitution?
questions.explain: The first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights.
questions.tip: Ten fingers, ten rights: the Bill of Rights is the first ten.

questions.q: Which right is protected by the First Amendment?
choices: The right to drive a car
The right to a free house
questions.explain: The First Amendment protects freedom of speech, religion, press, assembly and petition.
questions.tip: First comes first: speech, the right to speak your mind.

questions.q: Who is called the Father of the Constitution?
questions.explain: James Madison did so much planning and writing for the Constitution that he is called its father.
questions.tip: MADison MADe the Constitution plan.

questions.q: How many amendments does the Constitution have?
questions.explain: The Constitution has 27 amendments.
questions.tip: 27 amendments: 2 plus 7 is 9, like the number of Supreme Court justices.

questions.q: What is the short opening part of the Constitution called?
questions.explain: The Preamble is the introduction that explains the purposes of the Constitution.
questions.tip: PRE-amble: PRE means before, the part that comes before everything else.

questions.q: True or false: The Constitution can never be changed.
questions.explain: False! The Constitution can be changed through amendments. It has 27 of them.
questions.tip: The Constitution can be updated: 27 changes so far.

questions.q: In which year was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.explain: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776.
questions.tip: Spirit of '76: 1776 is the year America said goodbye to Britain.

questions.q: Who was the main writer of the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: Thomas Jefferson wrote most of the Declaration of Independence.
questions.tip: Jefferson's pen wrote the Declaration then.

questions.q: What did the Declaration of Independence do?
choices: Announced that the colonies were free from Great Britain
questions.explain: It declared that the 13 colonies were independent from Great Britain.
questions.tip: INDEPENDENCE means we don't depend on Britain anymore.

questions.q: From which country did the colonies declare independence?
questions.explain: The colonies declared independence from Great Britain.
questions.tip: Bye-bye, Britain! The colonies broke up with Great Britain.

questions.q: Which three rights does the Declaration of Independence name?
choices: Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
questions.explain: The Declaration says people have rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
questions.tip: L, L, H: Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.

questions.q: How many colonies declared independence in 1776?
questions.explain: The 13 colonies declared independence together.
questions.tip: 13 colonies, 13 stripes on the flag.

questions.q: Who was the king of Great Britain when the colonies declared independence?
questions.explain: King George III ruled Great Britain during the American Revolution.
questions.tip: George vs. George: King George III lost to General George Washington.

questions.q: Which group of colonial leaders approved the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: The Second Continental Congress, meeting in Philadelphia, approved the Declaration.
questions.tip: The Continental Congress gathered delegates from across the continent.

questions.q: Why were many colonists angry with Great Britain?
choices: They were taxed without having a vote in Parliament
Britain gave them too much freedom
Britain built them too many schools
They wanted a king of their own
questions.explain: Colonists objected to taxation without representation and other British policies.
questions.tip: No taxation without representation: no say, no pay!

questions.q: Which holiday celebrates the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: Independence Day, July 4, celebrates the adoption of the Declaration in 1776.
questions.tip: Independence Day celebrates the Declaration of Independence: same word, same day.

g35.name: How a bill becomes a law

questions.q: What is a bill?
choices: An idea for a new law
questions.explain: A bill is a proposed law that Congress considers.
questions.tip: A bill is a law's baby picture: a law before it grows up.

questions.q: Who can introduce a bill in Congress?
questions.explain: Only members of Congress can introduce bills, but anyone can suggest an idea to them.
questions.tip: Only lawmakers make law proposals.

questions.q: After a bill is introduced, where does it usually go first to be studied?
questions.explain: Committees study bills, hold hearings and decide whether to send them to a vote.
questions.tip: Committee: where a bill sits and gets a good look.

questions.q: Which parts of Congress must pass a bill before it goes to the President?
choices: Both the House and the Senate
questions.explain: Both the House and the Senate must pass the same bill.
questions.tip: Two houses, two yeses, then the President.

questions.q: What happens when the President signs a bill?
choices: It goes to the Supreme Court automatically
questions.explain: When the President signs a bill, it becomes law.
questions.tip: Signed, sealed, it's a law!

questions.q: If the President vetoes a bill, how can Congress still make it a law?
choices: By a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate
It can never become a law
questions.explain: Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
questions.tip: Two-thirds to override: Congress needs a super big team to win.

questions.q: Who signs bills to make them laws?
questions.explain: The President signs bills into law.
questions.tip: The President's pen turns bills into laws.

questions.q: Can ordinary citizens help a bill become a law?
choices: Yes, by contacting their members of Congress
Only if they live in the White House
questions.explain: Citizens can share ideas and opinions with their representatives and senators.
questions.tip: Write, call or email: your idea can travel to Congress.

questions.q: True or false: A bill passed only by the Senate becomes a law.
questions.explain: False. Both the House and the Senate must pass it, and then it goes to the President.
questions.tip: One house is half the job: both houses must say yes.

questions.q: What is it called when Congress votes to cancel a President's veto?
questions.explain: Overriding a veto takes a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.
questions.tip: OVERride: Congress rides over the veto.

questions.q: How many states are in the United States?
questions.explain: There are 50 states.
questions.tip: 50 states, 50 stars.

questions.q: What is the national government in Washington, D.C. called?
questions.explain: The national government is called the federal government.
questions.tip: Federal = national, the government for the whole nation.

questions.q: Who is the leader of a state's executive branch?
questions.explain: A governor leads each state.
questions.tip: Governor GOVERNs the state.

questions.q: Which of these is a power of the federal government?
questions.explain: Only the federal government prints money. States handle things like driver's licenses.
questions.tip: Big national jobs like printing money, declaring war and making treaties belong to the federal government.

questions.q: Which of these is a power of state governments?
questions.explain: States issue driver's licenses. The federal government declares war, prints money and makes treaties.
questions.tip: Your driver's license has your STATE's name on it.

questions.q: Does each state have its own constitution?
questions.explain: Every state has its own constitution, but it cannot go against the US Constitution.
questions.tip: Every state has its own rule book, but the US Constitution is the big boss.

questions.q: What is the city where a state's government meets called?
choices: The county seat of the nation
questions.explain: Each state has a capital city where its government meets.
questions.tip: Capital with an A for the city, like a capital A at the start of a sentence.

questions.q: Is Washington, D.C. a state?
choices: No, it is a federal district
Yes, it is the first state
No, it is part of Virginia
questions.explain: Washington, D.C. is a federal district, not a state.
questions.tip: D.C. stands for District of Columbia: a district, not a state.

questions.q: Who makes the laws for a state?
questions.explain: Each state has a legislature that makes state laws.
questions.tip: Each state has a mini-Congress: the state legislature.

questions.q: Which two countries border the United States?
questions.explain: Canada is to the north and Mexico is to the south.
questions.tip: Canada on the top, Mexico at the bottom, like a sandwich.

questions.q: How many articles are in the original Constitution?
questions.explain: The Constitution has seven articles, followed by its amendments.
questions.tip: Seven articles, like seven days of the week.

questions.q: Which article of the Constitution creates Congress?
questions.explain: Article I sets up the legislative branch, Congress.
questions.tip: LEJ in order: Article I Legislative, II Executive, III Judicial.

questions.q: Which article of the Constitution creates the presidency?
questions.explain: Article II sets up the executive branch.
questions.tip: Article II, second in line, just like the executive enforces after Congress makes laws.

questions.q: Which article of the Constitution creates the Supreme Court?
questions.explain: Article III sets up the judicial branch.
questions.tip: Article III: three for the third branch, the courts.

questions.q: Which article explains how to amend the Constitution?
questions.explain: Article V describes how amendments are proposed and ratified.
questions.tip: Article V: Five rhymes with revise.

questions.q: Article VI makes the Constitution and federal laws the supreme law of the land. What is this part called?
questions.explain: The Supremacy Clause in Article VI says federal law wins when it conflicts with state law.
questions.tip: Supremacy sounds like supreme: federal law is top dog.

questions.q: According to Article VII, how many states had to ratify the Constitution for it to take effect?
questions.explain: Ratification by nine of the thirteen states was required.
questions.tip: Nine to sign: 9 of 13 states had to say yes.

questions.q: Which article deals with how states treat each other, such as respecting each other's public records?
questions.explain: Article IV covers relations among the states, including the Full Faith and Credit Clause.
questions.tip: Article IV: four is for fellow states.

questions.q: What plan of government did the Constitution replace?
questions.explain: The Articles of Confederation created a weak national government and were replaced by the Constitution.
questions.tip: Articles of Confederation were Attempt One, the Constitution is Attempt Two.

questions.q: What was a major weakness of the Articles of Confederation?
choices: The President had too much power
The Supreme Court had too much power
questions.explain: Under the Articles, Congress could not tax and there was no national executive or court system.
questions.tip: No taxes, no money, no power: the Articles had empty pockets.

questions.q: The Great Compromise created a Congress with two houses. How is each state represented?
choices: Equally in the Senate and by population in the House
By land area in both houses
questions.explain: Each state gets two senators, while House seats are based on population.
questions.tip: Senate is the Same for every state; the House grows with how many people live there.

questions.q: Which amendment abolished slavery?
questions.explain: The 13th Amendment, ratified in 1865, abolished slavery.
questions.tip: 13 ended slavery: 13 set all free.

questions.q: Which amendment gave women the right to vote?
questions.explain: The 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920, protects women's right to vote.
questions.tip: 19 for women in 1920: 19 and 1920 share the 19.

questions.q: Which amendment lowered the voting age to 18?
questions.explain: The 26th Amendment, ratified in 1971, set the voting age at 18.
questions.tip: 26 makes 18 vote: 2 times 13 is 26, and 18 can finally vote.

questions.q: Which amendment says citizens cannot be denied the vote because of race or color?
questions.explain: The 15th Amendment, ratified in 1870, banned denying the vote based on race.
questions.tip: 13 freed, 14 made citizens, 15 let them vote: a 13-14-15 staircase to freedom.

questions.q: Which amendment says that all persons born in the United States are citizens and guarantees equal protection of the laws?
questions.explain: The 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868, defines citizenship and guarantees due process and equal protection.
questions.tip: 14 is for citizens and equal protection: 14 lines up everyone equally.

questions.q: Which amendment protects freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly and petition?
questions.explain: All five freedoms are in the First Amendment.
questions.tip: RAPPS: Religion, Assembly, Press, Petition, Speech, all in the First.

questions.q: Which amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures?
questions.explain: The 4th Amendment generally requires warrants based on probable cause.
questions.tip: Fourth for your door: police need a warrant to come through it.

questions.q: Pleading the Fifth means refusing to do what?
questions.explain: The 5th Amendment protects people from being forced to be witnesses against themselves.
questions.tip: Take the Fifth and keep your lips shut: you don't have to testify against yourself.

questions.q: Which amendment limits a President to being elected twice?
questions.explain: The 22nd Amendment, ratified in 1951, says no one can be elected President more than twice.
questions.tip: 22: two 2s, two terms.

questions.q: Which amendment says senators are elected directly by the people?
questions.explain: Before the 17th Amendment (1913), state legislatures chose senators.
questions.tip: 17: Seventeen, the people pick senators clean.

questions.q: Which amendment bans cruel and unusual punishment?
questions.explain: The 8th Amendment bans cruel and unusual punishment and excessive bail and fines.
questions.tip: Eight is great: no cruel punishment, no huge bail.

questions.q: What does checks and balances mean?
choices: Each branch can limit the power of the other branches
The government checks your bank balance
Only the President can make decisions
questions.explain: Checks and balances let each branch limit the others so no branch becomes too powerful.
questions.tip: Like a seesaw: each branch balances the others so none goes too high.

questions.q: How can the President check Congress?
questions.explain: The President can veto bills passed by Congress.
questions.tip: The President's veto is a big red NO stamp.

questions.q: How can Congress check a President's veto?
choices: Override it with a two-thirds vote in both houses
questions.explain: A two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate overrides a veto.
questions.tip: Two-thirds beats the veto: 67 senators and 290 representatives if everyone votes.

questions.q: Who nominates Supreme Court justices?
questions.explain: The President nominates federal judges, including Supreme Court justices.
questions.tip: President Picks, Senate Says yes: P then S.

questions.q: Who must confirm a President's nominee for the Supreme Court?
questions.explain: The Senate must give its advice and consent to confirm judicial nominees.
questions.tip: The Senate has the final say on judges: Senate Seats the justices.

questions.q: What fraction of the Senate must approve a treaty?
questions.explain: Treaties need the approval of two-thirds of the senators present.
questions.tip: Treaty takes two-thirds.

questions.q: Which part of Congress has the power to impeach, or formally charge, a federal official?
questions.explain: The House impeaches, and the Senate holds the trial.
questions.tip: House Hands up charges; Senate Sits as the jury.

questions.q: How many senators must vote to convict an impeached official and remove them from office?
questions.explain: Conviction in an impeachment trial requires two-thirds of the senators present.
questions.tip: Two-thirds to remove: the bar is high on purpose.

questions.q: What is the power of courts to strike down laws that violate the Constitution called?
questions.explain: Judicial review lets courts declare laws or actions unconstitutional.
questions.tip: Judges review the laws: judicial review.

questions.q: Which branch has the power to declare war?
questions.explain: The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war. The President is Commander in Chief.
questions.tip: Congress Declares, the President Commands.

questions.q: Which branch controls federal spending, sometimes called the power of the purse?
questions.explain: Congress must approve taxes and spending.
questions.tip: Congress holds the purse strings, like a parent with the allowance.

questions.q: What is federalism?
choices: Power is shared between the national government and the states
All power belongs to the national government
All power belongs to the states
questions.explain: In federalism, the national and state governments each have their own powers.
questions.tip: Federalism is a layer cake: national on top, states underneath, both with their own powers.

questions.q: Which amendment says powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people?
questions.explain: The 10th Amendment reserves powers to the states or the people.
questions.tip: 10th for the states: the last one in the Bill of Rights saves the rest for the states.

questions.q: Powers that both the federal and state governments have, like collecting taxes, are called what?
questions.explain: Concurrent powers are shared, such as taxing and making courts.
questions.tip: Concurrent means at the same time, like current flowing in two wires.

questions.q: Powers specifically listed in the Constitution for Congress are called what?
questions.explain: Enumerated, or expressed, powers are listed, mostly in Article I, Section 8.
questions.tip: Enumerated sounds like numbered: they are listed one by one.

questions.q: If a state law conflicts with a valid federal law, which one wins?
questions.explain: Under the Supremacy Clause, valid federal law overrides conflicting state law.
questions.tip: Federal beats state, like an ace beats a king.

questions.q: Which of these is a power of the federal government?
questions.explain: Making treaties is a federal power. The others are state or local.
questions.tip: Big national jobs like printing money, declaring war and making treaties belong to the federal government.

questions.q: Which of these is mainly a power of state governments?
questions.explain: USCIS lists providing schooling, police protection and driver's licenses as state powers.
questions.tip: Schools are state-run: S for state, S for school.

questions.q: The clause letting Congress make laws needed to carry out its listed powers is often called what?
questions.explain: The Necessary and Proper Clause is nicknamed the Elastic Clause because it stretches Congress's powers.
questions.tip: Elastic stretches like a rubber band, and so does Congress's power.

questions.q: Which type of government gives most power to the states, like under the Articles of Confederation?
questions.explain: In a confederation, states keep most power and the central government is weak.
questions.tip: Confederation = a club of states where the club itself is weak.

questions.q: Who leads a state's executive branch?
questions.explain: The governor heads the executive branch of a state.
questions.tip: Governor governs.

questions.q: Which is a responsibility that is only for United States citizens?
questions.explain: USCIS lists serving on a jury and voting in federal elections as responsibilities only for citizens.
questions.tip: Citizens only: Vote and Jury, V and J.

questions.q: Which is a right of everyone living in the United States, not just citizens?
questions.explain: Freedom of speech, religion, assembly and petition protect everyone in the US.
questions.tip: Speech is for everyone who's here.

questions.q: Which is a right only for United States citizens?
questions.explain: USCIS lists voting in federal elections and running for federal office as rights only for citizens.
questions.tip: To run for federal office, you must be a citizen first.

questions.q: What is the rule of law?
choices: Everyone must follow the law, including leaders
Only citizens must follow the law
The President is above the law
questions.explain: The rule of law means no one is above the law, including government leaders.
questions.tip: Rule of law: nobody is above it, not even the President.

questions.q: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
choices: The United States and the flag
questions.explain: The Pledge shows loyalty to the United States and to the flag.
questions.tip: Allegiance means loyalty: to the flag and the nation.

questions.q: At what age must most young men register for the Selective Service?
questions.explain: Men must register with the Selective Service at age 18 (between 18 and 26).
questions.tip: Turn 18, register: a birthday to-do.

questions.q: What does freedom of religion mean?
choices: You can practice any religion, or not practice a religion
Everyone must follow the same religion
Only leaders can choose a religion
questions.explain: Freedom of religion lets you practice any religion or none at all.
questions.tip: Freedom of religion means freedom to choose: any faith or none.

questions.q: Which of these is a way Americans can take part in their democracy?
questions.explain: USCIS lists voting, joining a civic group, contacting officials and helping campaigns, among others.
questions.tip: Participation is a team sport: write, vote, volunteer.

questions.q: What is the idea of self-government expressed in the first three words of the Constitution?
questions.explain: We the People means the people govern themselves.
questions.tip: We the People: WE run the show.

questions.q: What is the economic system of the United States?
questions.explain: USCIS accepts capitalist economy or market economy.
questions.tip: Market economy: like a giant farmers' market where people buy and sell freely.

questions.q: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
questions.explain: American Indians, or Native Americans, lived here long before Europeans arrived.
questions.tip: Native means born here: Native Americans were here first.

questions.q: What did the 12th Amendment change?
choices: Electors cast separate votes for President and Vice President
questions.explain: After the 1800 Jefferson-Burr electoral tie, the 12th Amendment (1804) required separate electoral votes for President and Vice President.
questions.tip: 12 split the ticket: President and VP get separate votes.

questions.q: Which amendment allows Congress to collect an income tax?
questions.explain: The 16th Amendment (1913) allows a federal income tax without apportioning it among the states.
questions.tip: 16 = income tax: sweet 16 gets a paycheck, and the IRS takes a cut.

questions.q: Which amendment established Prohibition, banning alcoholic beverages?
questions.explain: The 18th Amendment (1919) began Prohibition.
questions.tip: 18 banned the drink: ironic, since 18 sounds like a grown-up age.

questions.q: Which amendment repealed Prohibition?
questions.explain: The 21st Amendment (1933) repealed the 18th. It is the only amendment that repealed another.
questions.tip: 21 undid 18: 21 is today's drinking age too.

questions.q: Which amendment moved the start of presidential terms to January 20?
questions.explain: The 20th Amendment (1933), the Lame Duck Amendment, set January 20 for presidential terms and January 3 for Congress.
questions.tip: 20th Amendment, January 20: twenty and twenty.

questions.q: Which amendment gave Washington, D.C. electoral votes for President?
questions.explain: The 23rd Amendment (1961) gives D.C. electors, no more than the least populous state.
questions.tip: 23: D.C. gets 3, and 23 ends in 3.

questions.q: Which amendment banned poll taxes in federal elections?
questions.explain: The 24th Amendment (1964) prohibits poll taxes in federal elections.
questions.tip: 24: no paying at the poll; voting is free for all.

questions.q: Which amendment covers presidential disability and filling a Vice President vacancy?
questions.explain: The 25th Amendment (1967) covers succession, VP vacancies and presidential disability.
questions.tip: 25 keeps the presidency alive: a plan B for the top job.

questions.q: Which amendment delays any change in congressional pay until after the next House election?
questions.explain: The 27th Amendment was proposed in 1789 and finally ratified in 1992.
questions.tip: 27: the last amendment, and it took the longest, over 202 years.

questions.q: The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments are known together as what?
questions.explain: They were ratified between 1865 and 1870, after the Civil War, during Reconstruction.
questions.tip: Reconstruction rebuilt the nation after the Civil War: 13 free, 14 citizen, 15 vote.

questions.q: The 14th Amendment contains which two famous clauses limiting the states?
choices: Necessary and Proper and Take Care
questions.explain: Section 1 says no state shall deprive any person of life, liberty or property without due process, nor deny equal protection of the laws.
questions.tip: DP and EP: Due Process and Equal Protection.

questions.q: Which amendment protects against being tried twice for the same crime, known as double jeopardy?
questions.explain: The 5th Amendment includes protection against double jeopardy.
questions.tip: Fifth: you can't be tried twice, the Fifth won't let the court roll the dice twice.

questions.q: Which 1803 case established the Supreme Court's power of judicial review?
questions.explain: In Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall held that courts can strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution.
questions.tip: Marbury Made the court Mighty: M, M, M.

questions.q: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) upheld the national bank and ruled that what?
choices: Congress has implied powers and states cannot tax a federal bank
States can tax federal agencies freely
questions.explain: The Court relied on the Necessary and Proper Clause and the Supremacy Clause.
questions.tip: The power to tax is the power to destroy, so Maryland couldn't tax the bank.

questions.q: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), a case about steamboats, gave Congress broad power over what?
questions.explain: The Court read the Commerce Clause broadly to cover navigation between states.
questions.tip: Gibbons Governs Goods: steamboats moving goods between states.

questions.q: Which 1857 decision held that Black Americans could not be US citizens and was later overturned by the 14th Amendment?
questions.explain: Dred Scott also struck down the Missouri Compromise. The 14th Amendment's citizenship clause reversed it.
questions.tip: Dred Scott: a dreadful decision undone by the 14th Amendment.

questions.q: Which 1896 case upheld racial segregation under the separate but equal doctrine?
questions.explain: Plessy v. Ferguson allowed separate but equal facilities until it was rejected in Brown v. Board.
questions.tip: Plessy Permitted separation; Brown Broke it.

questions.q: What did Brown v. Board of Education (1954) decide?
choices: Racial segregation in public schools is unconstitutional
questions.explain: A unanimous Court led by Chief Justice Earl Warren held that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.
questions.tip: Brown v. BOARD: the Board of Education had to integrate schools.

questions.q: Because of Miranda v. Arizona (1966), police must do what before questioning a suspect in custody?
choices: Inform them of their rights, such as the right to remain silent
questions.explain: Miranda warnings protect the 5th Amendment right against self-incrimination.
questions.tip: You have the right to remain silent: that's the Miranda warning from every TV cop show.

questions.q: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) held that states must do what?
choices: Provide a lawyer to criminal defendants who cannot afford one
Hold all trials in federal court
questions.explain: The Court applied the 6th Amendment right to counsel to state felony trials.
questions.tip: Gideon's trumpet: a poor man wrote to the Court in pencil and won a lawyer for defendants who cannot afford one.

questions.q: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) applied which rule to state courts?
choices: The exclusionary rule: illegally obtained evidence cannot be used
The one person, one vote rule
questions.explain: Mapp applied the 4th Amendment exclusionary rule to the states.
questions.tip: Mapp: if police break the rules, the evidence goes off the map.

questions.q: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) protected students who wore black armbands to protest the Vietnam War. What did it hold?
choices: Students keep free speech rights at school unless their speech substantially disrupts
Schools may ban any political speech
Only teachers have free speech rights
questions.explain: The Court said students do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate.
questions.tip: Tinker's armbands: students keep their rights at the schoolhouse gate.

questions.q: In United States v. Nixon (1974), the Court ruled that the President had to do what?
questions.explain: The unanimous Court held executive privilege is not absolute. Nixon resigned soon after.
questions.tip: Nixon's tapes had to be handed over: no one is above the law.

questions.q: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for libel must prove what?
choices: Only that the statement was false
Nothing; the newspaper must prove truth
questions.explain: Public officials must show the statement was made knowing it was false or with reckless disregard for the truth.
questions.tip: Actual Malice: public officials need to show A M, knowing lies or reckless disregard.

questions.q: How many electors are in the Electoral College?
questions.explain: 435 representatives plus 100 senators plus 3 for D.C. equals 538.
questions.tip: 435 + 100 + 3 = 538: House plus Senate plus D.C.

questions.q: How many electoral votes does a candidate need to win the presidency?
questions.explain: 270 is a majority of 538.
questions.tip: Half of 538 is 269, plus one makes 270.

questions.q: How is the number of electors for each state determined?
choices: Its number of senators plus its number of representatives
questions.explain: Article II gives each state electors equal to its total seats in Congress.
questions.tip: Electors equal your state's seats in Congress: senators plus reps.

questions.q: How many electoral votes does Washington, D.C. have?
questions.explain: The 23rd Amendment gives D.C. as many electors as the least populous state, which is three.
questions.tip: The 23rd Amendment gave D.C. 3: look at the 3 at the end of 23.

questions.q: If no candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, who chooses the President?
questions.explain: Under the 12th Amendment, the House chooses, with each state delegation casting one vote.
questions.tip: House picks the President: H for House, H for Head of state.

questions.q: If no vice presidential candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, who chooses the Vice President?
questions.explain: The 12th Amendment gives that choice to the Senate.
questions.tip: Senate picks the VP, and the VP presides over the Senate: they go together.

questions.q: Which two states have split their electoral votes by congressional district?
questions.explain: Under their state laws, Maine and Nebraska have awarded two electors statewide and one per congressional district. Each state decides how to award its electors, so such laws can change.
questions.tip: Maine and Nebraska: M and N, side by side in the alphabet.

questions.q: On what day is the general election for President held?
choices: The Tuesday after the first Monday in November
questions.explain: Federal law sets Election Day as the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.
questions.tip: Tuesday after the first Monday: so Election Day is never November 1.

questions.q: On what date does a new presidential term begin?
questions.explain: The 20th Amendment sets noon on January 20. Before 1937, terms began March 4.
questions.tip: Inauguration on January 20: the 20th Amendment says so.

questions.q: True or false: A candidate can win the presidency without winning the national popular vote.
questions.explain: True. Because the winner is decided by electoral votes, this has happened several times, including 1876, 1888, 2000 and 2016.
questions.tip: Win states, not just votes: it's 270 electors that count.

questions.q: Can a member of Congress serve as an elector?
questions.explain: Article II says no senator, representative or federal officeholder may be an elector.
questions.tip: Electors must be outsiders: no federal officeholders allowed.

questions.q: How many US senators are there?
questions.explain: Each of the 50 states has two senators.
questions.tip: 100 senators: 2 per state times 50 states.

questions.q: How long is a senator's term?
questions.explain: Senators serve six-year terms.
questions.tip: Senators Six, Representatives Two, Presidents Four: 6-2-4.

questions.q: How many voting members are in the House of Representatives?
questions.explain: The House has 435 voting members.
questions.tip: 435: think 4-3-5, count down then up.

questions.q: How long is a representative's term?
questions.explain: Representatives serve two-year terms, so the whole House is elected every two years.
questions.tip: House = Hurry: they run every 2 years.

questions.q: About what share of the Senate is up for election every two years?
questions.explain: Senate terms are staggered so about one-third of seats are elected every two years.
questions.tip: 6-year terms split into three 2-year chunks: one-third each time.

questions.q: What is the minimum age to serve as a US senator?
questions.explain: Senators must be at least 30, citizens for nine years, and live in their state.
questions.tip: 25, 30, 35: House, Senate, President, climbing by fives.

questions.q: What is the minimum age to serve in the House of Representatives?
questions.explain: Representatives must be at least 25 and citizens for seven years.
questions.tip: 25 for the House: the youngest rung on the 25-30-35 ladder.

questions.q: Who is the President of the Senate and can break tie votes?
questions.explain: The Constitution makes the Vice President President of the Senate, voting only to break ties.
questions.tip: VP = Vote Picker in a tie.

questions.q: Who presides over the House of Representatives?
questions.explain: The House chooses its Speaker.
questions.tip: The Speaker speaks for the House.

questions.q: Bills to raise revenue, like tax bills, must start in which chamber?
questions.explain: The Origination Clause in Article I, Section 7 requires revenue bills to begin in the House.
questions.tip: House of the People pays the bills: money starts in the House.

questions.q: How often is the census taken to reapportion House seats among the states?
questions.explain: The Constitution requires a census every ten years.
questions.tip: Every decade, count every head: years ending in zero.

questions.q: Why do some states have more representatives than others?
choices: Because of the state's land area
questions.explain: House seats are apportioned by population.
questions.tip: More people, more reps: it's a head count.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of the Federalist Papers?
choices: To persuade people to ratify the Constitution
To create the Bill of Rights
questions.explain: The essays argued for ratifying the new Constitution, especially in New York.
questions.tip: Federalists were FOR the Constitution: they wrote to sell it.

questions.q: Which three men wrote the Federalist Papers?
choices: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay
Thomas Jefferson, John Adams and Ben Franklin
George Washington, Patrick Henry and George Mason
Samuel Adams, John Hancock and Paul Revere
questions.explain: Hamilton, Madison and Jay wrote the essays.
questions.tip: HMJ: Hamilton, Madison, Jay, like Ham, Mad and Jay.

questions.q: Under what pen name were the Federalist Papers published?
questions.explain: All 85 essays were signed Publius, after a founder of the Roman Republic.
questions.tip: Publius sounds like public: they wrote to the public.

questions.q: How many essays make up the Federalist Papers?
questions.explain: There are 85 essays, published in 1787 and 1788.
questions.tip: 85 essays: 8 and 5 add up to 13, like the 13 states they wanted to convince.

questions.q: Who wrote the most Federalist essays?
questions.explain: Hamilton wrote about 51, Madison about 29 and Jay 5.
questions.tip: Hamilton was the heavy hitter: about 51 of the 85 essays, more than half.

questions.q: Federalist No. 10 argues that a large republic helps control what?
questions.explain: Madison argued that a large republic makes it hard for any one faction to dominate.
questions.tip: Ten for factions: big republic, many groups, no one wins it all.

questions.q: Federalist No. 51 says ambition must be made to counteract ambition. What idea does it defend?
choices: Checks and balances and separation of powers
questions.explain: Madison argued that each branch should have the means to resist encroachment by the others.
questions.tip: 51 = checks and balances: if men were angels, no government would be necessary.

questions.q: Federalist No. 78 describes which branch as the least dangerous?
questions.explain: Hamilton wrote that the judiciary has neither force nor will, only judgment.
questions.tip: 78: courts have no sword and no purse, only judgment.

questions.q: What were opponents of ratifying the Constitution called?
questions.explain: Anti-Federalists, such as Patrick Henry and George Mason, feared a strong central government.
questions.tip: ANTI means against: Anti-Federalists were against the Constitution.

questions.q: What concession did supporters of the Constitution make to win over many Anti-Federalists?
questions.explain: The promise of a Bill of Rights helped win ratification; it was ratified in 1791.
questions.tip: Anti-Federalists said no rights, no deal, so the Bill of Rights sealed it.

questions.q: Is the power of judicial review explicitly stated in the text of the Constitution?
choices: No, it was established by Marbury v. Madison
questions.explain: Judicial review is not spelled out in the text; Marshall reasoned it from the nature of a written constitution and Article III.
questions.tip: Not in the text, but in Marbury's context.

questions.q: Article III limits federal courts to hearing actual what?
questions.explain: The case-or-controversy requirement is why federal courts do not issue advisory opinions.
questions.tip: Real cases, real controversies: no what-ifs.

questions.q: Under Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992), the three elements of Article III standing are injury in fact, causation and what?
questions.explain: A plaintiff must show a concrete injury, fairly traceable to the defendant, likely to be redressed by a favorable decision.
questions.tip: Standing is I-C-R: Injury, Causation, Redressability, I see red.

questions.q: In which cases does the Supreme Court have original jurisdiction under Article III?
choices: Cases affecting ambassadors and those in which a state is a party
All cases involving more than $1 million
questions.explain: Article III, Section 2 limits original jurisdiction to these categories; other jurisdiction is appellate.
questions.tip: States and ambassadors go straight to the top.

questions.q: Which 1958 case held that state officials are bound by Supreme Court interpretations of the Constitution?
questions.explain: Arising from Little Rock school desegregation, Cooper v. Aaron declared that Brown bound the states.
questions.tip: Cooper says the states must cooperate with the Court.

questions.q: The political question doctrine holds that courts should not decide which issues?
choices: Those committed to other branches or lacking manageable judicial standards
questions.explain: Baker v. Carr (1962) set out the factors, while holding that legislative apportionment was justiciable.
questions.tip: Some questions belong to the political branches, not the courts.

questions.q: Under Article III, federal judges hold office during what?
questions.explain: Good-behavior tenure, along with protection against salary cuts, secures judicial independence.
questions.tip: Good behavior equals a lifetime job, as long as they behave.

questions.q: Ex parte McCardle (1869) is often cited for Congress's power to do what?
choices: Limit the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction
Overrule Supreme Court decisions by statute
questions.explain: The Exceptions Clause lets Congress make exceptions to appellate jurisdiction; McCardle upheld a repeal mid-case.
questions.tip: McCardle: Congress can take a card out of the Court's appellate deck.

questions.q: What is the term for the principle that courts should follow their prior decisions?
questions.explain: Stare decisis means to stand by things decided.
questions.tip: Stare decisis: stand by what's decided, like staring at the old rulebook.

questions.q: How do most cases reach the Supreme Court today?
choices: By a writ of certiorari, which the Court grants at its discretion
By automatic appeal from every federal court
questions.explain: The Court grants certiorari in a small fraction of petitions; four justices must agree to hear a case.
questions.tip: Rule of four: four justices say yes, cert is granted.

questions.q: Which two amendments contain Due Process Clauses?
questions.explain: The 5th binds the federal government; the 14th binds the states.
questions.tip: 5 for the feds, 14 for the states.

questions.q: What is the difference between procedural and substantive due process?
choices: Procedural concerns fair procedures; substantive protects certain rights from government interference regardless of procedure
Procedural applies to states; substantive applies only to the federal government
Substantive applies only to criminal cases
questions.explain: Procedural due process asks how government acts; substantive asks whether it may act at all.
questions.tip: Procedural = How; Substantive = Whether.

questions.q: Barron v. Baltimore (1833) held that the Bill of Rights applied to whom?
questions.explain: Barron held the Bill of Rights did not limit states, which set the stage for later incorporation through the 14th Amendment.
questions.tip: Barron barred the Bill of Rights from binding the states.

questions.q: Making Bill of Rights protections apply to the states through the 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause is called what?
questions.explain: The Court has used selective incorporation, applying rights one by one.
questions.tip: Incorporate = put into the body: rights put into the 14th.

questions.q: Which 1925 case assumed that freedom of speech applies to the states through the 14th Amendment?
questions.explain: Gitlow is widely seen as the start of incorporating First Amendment rights.
questions.tip: Gitlow got the ball rolling on incorporation.

questions.q: Lochner v. New York (1905) struck down a limit on bakers' working hours based on what idea?
choices: Liberty of contract under substantive due process
questions.explain: The Lochner era ended with West Coast Hotel v. Parrish (1937), which upheld a minimum wage law.
questions.tip: Lochner's bakers baked up liberty of contract.

questions.q: Mathews v. Eldridge (1976) set a balancing test for what?
choices: How much process is due before the government deprives someone of a protected interest
When police may search a car
Whether a law is a valid tax
questions.explain: It weighs the private interest, the risk of error and the value of more safeguards, and the government's interest.
questions.tip: Mathews does the math: weigh three factors for due process.

questions.q: What level of scrutiny do courts apply to government classifications based on race?
questions.explain: Racial classifications must be narrowly tailored to a compelling government interest.
questions.tip: Race gets the strictest look: strict scrutiny.

questions.q: Craig v. Boren (1976) applied which standard to sex-based classifications?
questions.explain: Sex classifications must be substantially related to an important government objective.
questions.tip: Craig's in the middle: intermediate scrutiny for sex.

questions.q: Most economic regulations are reviewed under which deferential standard?
questions.explain: A law survives if it is rationally related to a legitimate government interest.
questions.tip: Rational basis: just needs a reason that makes sense.

questions.q: The 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause applies to states. How did Bolling v. Sharpe (1954) apply equal protection to the federal government?
choices: Through the 5th Amendment's Due Process Clause
questions.explain: Bolling, a companion case to Brown, struck down school segregation in Washington, D.C.
questions.tip: Bolling went backward: equal protection reverse-incorporated into the Fifth.

questions.q: The Slaughter-House Cases (1873) gave a narrow reading to which 14th Amendment clause?
questions.explain: The narrow reading left later rights protection to the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses.
questions.tip: Slaughter-House slaughtered Privileges or Immunities.

college.name: The Commerce Clause and federal power

questions.q: The Commerce Clause gives Congress power to regulate commerce with foreign nations, among the several states, and with whom?
questions.explain: Article I, Section 8, Clause 3 lists foreign, interstate and Indian commerce.
questions.tip: Three Fs of commerce: Foreign, Fellow states and First nations (tribes).

questions.q: Wickard v. Filburn (1942) upheld federal limits on wheat a farmer grew for his own use based on what reasoning?
choices: In the aggregate, such activity substantially affects interstate commerce
The wheat was sold across state lines
Farming is a federal property right
questions.explain: Wickard's aggregation principle greatly expanded the reach of the Commerce Clause.
questions.tip: Wickard's wheat: one farmer's crop adds up across all farms.

questions.q: Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964) upheld which law under the Commerce Clause?
choices: The Civil Rights Act of 1964's ban on discrimination in public accommodations
questions.explain: The Court found racial discrimination by motels serving travelers burdened interstate commerce.
questions.tip: Heart of Atlanta: travelers cross states, so motels touch commerce.

questions.q: United States v. Lopez (1995) was significant because the Court did what?
choices: Struck down a federal law as exceeding the Commerce Clause for the first time in nearly 60 years
Expanded the Commerce Clause to all activity
questions.explain: The Gun-Free School Zones Act regulated non-economic activity without a substantial effect on interstate commerce.
questions.tip: Lopez lopped off a federal law: guns near schools aren't commerce.

questions.q: United States v. Morrison (2000) struck down which provision as beyond Congress's commerce power?
choices: The civil remedy in the Violence Against Women Act
questions.explain: The Court held that gender-motivated violence was not economic activity Congress could regulate under the Commerce Clause.
questions.tip: Morrison followed Lopez: non-economic means not commerce.

questions.q: What is the dormant Commerce Clause?
choices: An implied limit on states discriminating against or unduly burdening interstate commerce
A clause that has never been used
Congress's power to ban all trade
A clause repealed by the 21st Amendment
questions.explain: Courts infer it from the grant of commerce power to Congress.
questions.tip: Dormant means sleeping: the clause still bites states while Congress sleeps.

questions.q: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), the Court upheld the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate under which power?
questions.explain: A majority said the mandate exceeded the commerce power but could be sustained as a tax.
questions.tip: Not commerce, but a tax: the mandate survived as a tax.

questions.q: South Dakota v. Dole (1987) upheld conditioning some federal highway funds on states adopting what?
questions.explain: The Court approved this use of the Spending Clause and set limits on conditional grants.
questions.tip: Dole doles out highway dollars with strings: drinking age 21.

questions.q: Which clause did McCulloch v. Maryland rely on to find that Congress could charter a bank?
choices: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
questions.explain: Marshall read necessary as convenient or useful, not absolutely indispensable.
questions.tip: Necessary and Proper = the Elastic Clause stretches to a bank.

questions.q: Gonzales v. Raich (2005) held that Congress could regulate what under the Commerce Clause?
choices: Marijuana grown at home for personal medical use
questions.explain: Relying on Wickard, the Court found home-grown marijuana part of a national market Congress could regulate.
questions.tip: Raich is Wickard with weed: home-grown still affects the market.

questions.q: Which French thinker's writings on separating legislative, executive and judicial power influenced the framers?
questions.explain: Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) is cited in Federalist No. 47.
questions.tip: Montesquieu: the three-branch mon-sieur.

questions.q: Youngstown Sheet and Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952) held that President Truman could not do what?
choices: Seize steel mills without congressional authorization
questions.explain: The Court rejected the seizure, made during the Korean War to avert a strike.
questions.tip: Truman couldn't steal the steel.

questions.q: In Justice Jackson's Youngstown concurrence, presidential power is at its lowest ebb when the President acts how?
choices: In a way incompatible with the expressed or implied will of Congress
questions.explain: Jackson's three categories are authorization, silence (the zone of twilight) and opposition.
questions.tip: Jackson's tide: high with Congress, twilight in silence, low ebb against Congress.

questions.q: INS v. Chadha (1983) struck down the one-house legislative veto because it violated what?
questions.explain: Legislative action must pass both houses and be presented to the President.
questions.tip: Chadha: no shortcuts, two houses plus the President.

questions.q: Clinton v. City of New York (1998) struck down which presidential power?
questions.explain: The Line Item Veto Act let the President cancel parts of signed laws, violating the Presentment Clause.
questions.tip: No line-item veto: the President signs the whole bill or none.

questions.q: Morrison v. Olson (1988) upheld what?
choices: The independent counsel provisions of the Ethics in Government Act
questions.explain: The Court ruled 7 to 1, with Justice Scalia's lone dissent defending a strong unitary executive.
questions.tip: Morrison v. Olson: 7 to 1, with Scalia's famous wolf dissent.

questions.q: The nondelegation doctrine requires that when Congress delegates authority, it provide what?
questions.explain: The intelligible principle test comes from J.W. Hampton v. United States (1928).
questions.tip: Delegate with an IP: an Intelligible Principle.

questions.q: In which year did the Supreme Court strike down federal statutes on nondelegation grounds, in Panama Refining and Schechter Poultry?
questions.explain: Both 1935 cases involved the National Industrial Recovery Act.
questions.tip: 1935: nondelegation struck twice, both New Deal laws.

questions.q: The War Powers Resolution of 1973 generally requires the President to withdraw forces after how many days without congressional authorization?
choices: 60 days, plus up to 30 for withdrawal
questions.explain: It also requires notifying Congress within 48 hours. It was passed over President Nixon's veto.
questions.tip: 48 hours to tell, 60 days to stay, 30 more to pull away.

questions.q: The Constitution divides war powers. Which power does Article II give the President?
choices: Commander in Chief of the armed forces
Making rules for the armed forces
questions.explain: Article I gives Congress the power to declare war, raise armies and regulate the military.
questions.tip: Congress declares, the President commands.

questions.q: What does the Take Care Clause in Article II require?
choices: That the President take care that the laws be faithfully executed
That Congress take care of federal property
That courts take care of the poor
That states take care of elections
questions.explain: It is central to debates over presidential enforcement discretion.
questions.tip: Take care to execute: the President's job description in a phrase.

questions.q: The 11th Amendment (1795) was a response to which Supreme Court case?
choices: Pollock v. Farmers' Loan and Trust
questions.explain: Chisholm allowed a citizen of another state to sue Georgia; the 11th Amendment limited such suits.
questions.tip: Chisholm chilled: the 11th shielded states from suits.

questions.q: Which election prompted the 12th Amendment?
choices: 1800, when Jefferson and Burr tied in electoral votes
1824, when the House chose John Quincy Adams
questions.explain: Electors originally cast two votes without distinguishing President from Vice President.
questions.tip: 1800's tie between Jefferson and Burr led to the 12th, a deal sealed for sure.

questions.q: The 16th Amendment overturned the effect of which 1895 case striking down a federal income tax?
choices: Pollock v. Farmers' Loan and Trust Co.
questions.explain: Pollock held an income tax on property income was a direct tax requiring apportionment.
questions.tip: Pollock polled out the income tax; the 16th brought it back.

questions.q: The 21st Amendment is unique because it was ratified by what method?
questions.explain: It is the only amendment ratified by state conventions, an option allowed by Article V.
questions.tip: 21: the one done by conventions, not legislatures.

questions.q: Which amendment was proposed in 1789 but not ratified until 1992?
questions.explain: The congressional pay amendment was one of Madison's original proposals; a student-led campaign revived it in the 1980s.
questions.tip: 27 waited over 202 years: the slowest amendment ever.

questions.q: The 22nd Amendment (1951) followed which President's four election victories?
questions.explain: FDR won in 1932, 1936, 1940 and 1944, breaking the two-term tradition begun by Washington.
questions.tip: FDR won four, so 22 said two and no more.

questions.q: The 25th Amendment (1967) was first used under Section 2 to fill a vice presidential vacancy with whom?
questions.explain: Nixon nominated Ford in 1973 after Agnew resigned; Ford later named Rockefeller the same way.
questions.tip: Ford was the first VP nobody elected, thanks to the 25th.

questions.q: Article V provides two ways to propose amendments: by two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or by what?
choices: A convention called on application of two-thirds of state legislatures
questions.explain: No amendment has ever been proposed by an Article V convention.
questions.tip: Two doors in: Congress or a Convention, C and C.

questions.q: How many states must ratify an amendment for it to become part of the Constitution?
questions.explain: With 50 states, that means 38.
questions.tip: 38 of 50 equals three-fourths: a supermajority of states.

questions.q: Which amendment was the first to be repealed by another amendment?
questions.explain: The 21st Amendment repealed the 18th in 1933. No other amendment has been repealed.
questions.tip: 18 was the only one ever undone, by 21.

questions.q: The Reconstruction Amendments were ratified during which span of years?
questions.tip: Five years, three amendments: 1865 to 1870.

questions.q: What is the supreme law of the land?
questions.explain: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land.
questions.tip: The Constitution is the boss of all the laws.

questions.q: What does the Constitution do?
choices: Sets up the government and protects basic rights of Americans
Lists the names of the 50 states
questions.explain: USCIS accepts: sets up the government, defines the government, protects basic rights of Americans.
questions.tip: The Constitution is the blueprint: it builds the government and protects rights.

questions.q: The idea of self-government is in the first three words of the Constitution. What are these words?
questions.explain: We the People expresses that the people govern themselves.
questions.tip: We the People: the people are the bosses.

questions.q: What is an amendment?
choices: A change or addition to the Constitution
questions.explain: An amendment changes or adds to the Constitution.
questions.tip: Amend means mend or fix: an amendment changes the Constitution.

questions.q: What do we call the first ten amendments to the Constitution?
questions.explain: The first ten amendments are the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791.
questions.tip: Ten fingers, ten rights: the Bill of Rights is the first ten.

questions.q: How many amendments does the Constitution have?
questions.explain: There are 27 amendments.
questions.tip: 27 amendments: 2 plus 7 is 9, like the number of Supreme Court justices.

questions.q: What did the Declaration of Independence do?
choices: Announced and declared independence from Great Britain
questions.explain: It announced that the colonies were free from Great Britain.
questions.tip: INDEPENDENCE means we don't depend on Britain anymore.

questions.q: What are two rights in the Declaration of Independence?
