questions.explain: The Declaration names life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
questions.tip: Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness: L, L, H.

questions.q: What is the economic system in the United States?
questions.explain: USCIS accepts capitalist economy or market economy.
questions.tip: Capitalism and market: buying and selling in a free marketplace.

questions.q: What is the rule of law?
choices: Everyone must follow the law; leaders and government must obey the law
The President decides what the law is
Only citizens must obey the law
questions.explain: No one is above the law.
questions.tip: Rule of law: nobody is above it, not even the President.

questions.q: What stops one branch of government from becoming too powerful?
questions.explain: USCIS accepts checks and balances or separation of powers.
questions.tip: Checks and balances: every branch keeps the others in check.

questions.q: Who is in charge of the executive branch?
questions.explain: The President heads the executive branch.
questions.tip: The President executes the laws.

questions.q: Who makes federal laws?
questions.explain: USCIS accepts Congress, Senate and House, or the US or national legislature.
questions.tip: Congress makes laws: think CongresS and StatuteS.

questions.q: We elect a US senator for how many years?
questions.explain: Senators serve six-year terms.
questions.tip: Six for Senators: S and S.

questions.q: We elect a US representative for how many years?
questions.explain: Representatives serve two-year terms.
questions.tip: Representatives: 2 years, they're always running.

questions.q: We elect a President for how many years?
questions.explain: A presidential term is four years.
questions.tip: Four years, like a high school or college term.

questions.q: Who does a US senator represent?
choices: Only the people who voted for them
questions.explain: A senator represents everyone in the state.
questions.tip: Senators speak for the whole state.

questions.q: In what month do we vote for President?
questions.explain: Presidential elections are held in November.
questions.tip: Remember, remember, vote in November.

questions.q: If the President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
questions.explain: The Vice President is first in the line of succession.
questions.tip: VP = Very next President.

questions.q: If both the President and the Vice President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
choices: The President pro tempore of the Senate
questions.explain: Under the Presidential Succession Act, the Speaker of the House is next after the Vice President.
questions.tip: President, VP, Speaker: third in line.

questions.q: Who is the Commander in Chief of the military?
choices: The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs
questions.explain: Article II makes the President Commander in Chief.
questions.tip: Chief of the country, chief of the military.

questions.q: What does the President's Cabinet do?
questions.explain: Cabinet members head executive departments and advise the President.
questions.tip: A Cabinet holds the President's advisors, like a cabinet holds dishes.

questions.q: What does the judicial branch do?
choices: Reviews laws, explains laws and resolves disputes
questions.explain: USCIS also accepts: decides if a law goes against the Constitution.
questions.tip: Judges judge: review, explain, resolve.

questions.q: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the federal government. What is one?
questions.explain: Federal powers include printing money, declaring war, creating an army and making treaties.
questions.tip: Big national stuff: war, money, army, treaties.

questions.q: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the states. What is one?
questions.explain: State powers include schooling, police, safety, driver's licenses and zoning.
questions.tip: Local stuff: schools, police, licenses, zoning.

questions.q: There are four amendments to the Constitution about who can vote. Which describes one of them?
choices: Citizens must pass a literacy test
Voters must pay a poll tax
questions.explain: The voting amendments: race (15th), women (19th), no poll tax (24th), age 18 (26th).
questions.tip: 15, 19, 24, 26: race, women, no poll tax, age 18.

questions.q: What is one responsibility that is only for United States citizens?
questions.explain: Serving on a jury and voting in federal elections are responsibilities only for citizens.
questions.tip: Jury and vote: what citizens alone owe.

questions.q: What is one promise you make when you become a United States citizen?
choices: Defend the Constitution and laws of the United States
questions.explain: The oath also includes giving up loyalty to other countries, obeying the laws and serving the nation if needed.
questions.tip: The oath is a promise to defend, obey and serve.

questions.q: How old do citizens have to be to vote for President?
questions.explain: The 26th Amendment set the voting age at 18.
questions.tip: 18: old enough to vote.

questions.q: When is the last day you can send in federal income tax forms, in a typical year?
questions.explain: USCIS accepts April 15. The deadline shifts when April 15 falls on a weekend or holiday.
questions.tip: April 15: Tax Day, right in the middle of April.

questions.q: When must all men register for the Selective Service?
questions.explain: Men must register between ages 18 and 26.
questions.tip: 18 to 26: register when you turn 18.

questions.q: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: Jefferson was the principal author.
questions.tip: Jefferson, the Declaration's pen.

questions.q: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.explain: The Continental Congress adopted it on July 4, 1776.
questions.tip: July 4, 1776: the nation's birthday.

questions.q: When was the Constitution written?
questions.explain: It was written at the Constitutional Convention in 1787.
questions.tip: 1787: eleven years after 1776.

questions.q: The Federalist Papers supported passage of the Constitution. Name one of the writers.
questions.explain: The writers were Madison, Alexander Hamilton and John Jay, under the name Publius.
questions.tip: Hamilton, Madison, Jay: HMJ.

questions.q: What is one thing Benjamin Franklin is famous for?
choices: He was the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention
He wrote the Bill of Rights
He was the first Chief Justice
questions.explain: USCIS also accepts: diplomat, first Postmaster General, writer of Poor Richard's Almanac, started the first free libraries.
questions.tip: Franklin, at 81, was the oldest founder in the room.

questions.q: Who is the Father of Our Country?
questions.explain: George Washington is called the Father of Our Country.
questions.tip: George Washington, father of the nation, face on the dollar.

questions.q: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
questions.explain: The Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled the size of the country.
questions.tip: Louisiana sounds like Louis, the French kings' name.

questions.q: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
questions.explain: USCIS accepts the War of 1812, Mexican-American War, Civil War and Spanish-American War.
questions.tip: 1800s: 1812, Mexican-American, Civil, Spanish-American.

questions.q: What was one important thing that Abraham Lincoln did?
choices: Freed the slaves with the Emancipation Proclamation
Led the US in World War I
questions.explain: USCIS also accepts: saved or preserved the Union, led the US during the Civil War.
questions.tip: Honest Abe freed the slaves and saved the Union.

questions.q: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
choices: Freed the slaves in the Confederate states
Gave women the right to vote
questions.explain: Issued in 1863, it declared slaves in Confederate-held areas free.
questions.tip: Emancipate means set free.

questions.q: What did Susan B. Anthony do?
choices: Led troops in the Civil War
Was the first woman on the Supreme Court
questions.explain: She was a leader for women's rights and civil rights.
questions.tip: Susan B. fought for women's right to vote: she's on a dollar coin.

questions.q: Who was President during World War I?
questions.explain: Woodrow Wilson led the country during World War I.
questions.tip: Wilson, W for World War I.

questions.q: Who was President during the Great Depression and World War II?
questions.explain: Franklin D. Roosevelt served from 1933 until his death in 1945.
questions.tip: FDR: Fought Depression and Rivals in World War II.

questions.q: Before he was President, Eisenhower was a general. What war was he in?
questions.explain: Eisenhower was Supreme Allied Commander in Europe during World War II.
questions.tip: Ike liked D-Day: World War II general.

questions.q: During the Cold War, what was the main concern of the United States?
questions.explain: The Cold War was a rivalry with the Soviet Union and the spread of communism.
questions.tip: Cold War, Communism: C and C.

questions.q: What did Martin Luther King, Jr. do?
choices: Fought for civil rights and equality for all Americans
Was the first Black Supreme Court justice
questions.explain: He was a leader of the civil rights movement.
questions.tip: I Have a Dream: equality for all.

questions.q: What major event happened on September 11, 2001, in the United States?
choices: The end of World War II
questions.explain: Terrorists hijacked planes and attacked New York City and Washington, D.C.; another plane crashed in Pennsylvania.
questions.tip: 9/11: terrorists attacked the United States.

questions.q: Name one US territory.
questions.explain: Territories include Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands. Hawaii and Alaska are states.
questions.tip: Puerto Rico: a territory, not a state.

questions.q: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?
questions.explain: The stripes represent the 13 original colonies.
questions.tip: 13 stripes for 13 colonies.

questions.q: What is the name of the national anthem?
questions.explain: The Star-Spangled Banner became the official anthem in 1931.
questions.tip: Star-Spangled Banner: the flag still waved over Fort McHenry.

questions.q: What group of people was taken to America and sold as slaves?
questions.explain: Enslaved Africans were brought to America against their will.
questions.tip: Africans were brought to America in chains.

questions.q: How long is a US senator's term?
questions.explain: Six years; about one-third of the Senate is elected every two years.
questions.tip: Senators Six: S and S.

questions.q: How long is a term for a member of the House of Representatives?
questions.explain: Two years; every House seat is up each even-numbered year.
questions.tip: House Hurries: every 2 years.

questions.q: How long do federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, serve?
choices: During good behavior, effectively for life
questions.explain: Article III judges have no fixed term and can be removed only by impeachment and conviction.
questions.tip: Good behavior is forever: life tenure.

questions.q: What does the First Amendment protect?
choices: Religion, speech, press, assembly and petition
The right to a jury trial
questions.explain: Five freedoms: religion, speech, press, peaceable assembly and petitioning the government.
questions.tip: RAPPS: Religion, Assembly, Press, Petition, Speech.

questions.q: What does the Second Amendment protect?
choices: The right to keep and bear arms
The right to a speedy trial
questions.explain: The Second Amendment protects the right to keep and bear arms.
questions.tip: Two arms, Second Amendment: the right to bear arms.

questions.q: What does the Third Amendment protect against?
choices: Being forced to quarter soldiers in your home in peacetime
questions.explain: No soldier may be quartered in a house without the owner's consent in peacetime, or in wartime except as law prescribes.
questions.tip: Third: no soldiers on your couch.

questions.q: What does the Fourth Amendment protect against?
questions.explain: Warrants require probable cause and must describe the place and items to be searched or seized.
questions.tip: Fourth for your door: no unreasonable searches.

questions.q: Which protections are in the Fifth Amendment?
choices: Grand jury, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination, due process and just compensation
Speedy and public trial and right to counsel
Right to a jury in civil cases
questions.explain: The 5th also includes the Takings Clause: private property cannot be taken for public use without just compensation.
questions.tip: Five protections in the Fifth: grand jury, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, due process, takings.

questions.q: What does the Sixth Amendment guarantee in criminal cases?
choices: A speedy and public trial by an impartial jury, and the assistance of counsel
questions.explain: It also includes the rights to be informed of the charges and to confront witnesses.
questions.tip: Six for a speedy trial: quick, public, fair, with a lawyer.

questions.q: What does the Seventh Amendment guarantee?
choices: A jury trial in many civil cases
A jury trial in criminal cases
questions.explain: It preserves the right to a civil jury where the value in controversy exceeds twenty dollars.
questions.tip: Seven for civil: jury in lawsuits over $20.

questions.q: What does the Eighth Amendment prohibit?
choices: Excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishment
questions.explain: The 8th Amendment limits punishments and bail.
questions.tip: Eight is great: no cruel punishment, no crazy bail.

questions.q: What does the Ninth Amendment say?
choices: Listing certain rights does not deny other rights retained by the people
Powers not delegated are reserved to the states
questions.explain: The 9th Amendment guards against reading the Bill of Rights as a complete list of rights.
questions.tip: Nine: there are more rights than the list.

questions.q: What does the Tenth Amendment say?
choices: Powers not delegated to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people
questions.explain: The 10th Amendment is the basis of reserved state powers.
questions.tip: Ten: the leftovers go to the states and people.

questions.q: What are the qualifications to be President?
choices: Natural-born citizen, at least 35, and 14 years a US resident
Citizen for 7 years and at least 25
Citizen for 9 years and at least 30
questions.explain: Article II, Section 1 sets these requirements.
questions.tip: 35, 14, born here: President's three rules.

questions.q: In what year was the Bill of Rights ratified?
questions.explain: It was ratified on December 15, 1791.
questions.tip: 1791: four years after 1787.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of times a person can be elected President?
questions.explain: Under the 22nd Amendment. Someone who served more than two years of another's term can be elected only once.
questions.tip: 22nd Amendment: two terms, two 2s.

questions.q: What vote does Congress need to override a presidential veto?
choices: A simple majority of both houses
questions.explain: Article I, Section 7 requires two-thirds of each house.
questions.tip: Two-thirds in both: a supermajority beats a veto.

questions.q: How many states must ratify a constitutional amendment?
questions.explain: Article V requires ratification by three-fourths of the states.
questions.tip: 38 of 50: three-fourths of the states.

questions.q: Who presides over the Senate trial when a President is impeached?
questions.explain: Article I, Section 3 says the Chief Justice presides when the President is tried.
questions.tip: The Chief Justice presides, not the VP, who could become President.

questions.q: How many days (excluding Sundays) does the President have to sign or veto a bill?
questions.explain: If the President does nothing for ten days while Congress is in session, the bill becomes law without a signature.
questions.tip: Ten days to decide: count on your fingers.

questions.q: What is a pocket veto?
choices: A bill dies when Congress adjourns and the President does not sign it within ten days
The President vetoes a bill secretly
A veto of only part of a bill
questions.explain: Because Congress has adjourned, the bill cannot be returned and so does not become law.
questions.tip: Pocket veto: the President pockets the bill and it dies when Congress leaves.

questions.q: How many electoral votes are needed to win the presidency?
questions.explain: A majority of the 538 electors.
questions.tip: 270 to win.

questions.q: What fraction of the Senate must approve a treaty?
questions.explain: Article II, Section 2.
questions.tip: Treaty takes two-thirds.

questions.q: Which crime is defined in the Constitution itself?
questions.explain: Article III defines treason as levying war against the US or adhering to its enemies, giving them aid and comfort.
questions.tip: Treason is the only crime the Constitution spells out.

questions.q: Who is the President of the Senate?
questions.explain: The Vice President presides and votes only to break ties.
questions.tip: VP presides, VP decides ties.

questions.q: Which writ, protected in Article I, lets a prisoner challenge unlawful detention?
questions.explain: It may be suspended only when public safety requires it in cases of rebellion or invasion.
questions.tip: Habeas corpus: you have the body, so show why you hold it.

questions.q: What is the Constitution's minimum age for a member of the House, the Senate and the presidency, in that order?
questions.explain: Articles I and II set these minimums.
questions.tip: 25, 30, 35: climb by fives from House to President.

questions.q: On what date was the Constitution signed?
questions.explain: September 17 is observed as Constitution Day and Citizenship Day.
questions.tip: September 17: Constitution Day.

questions.q: Which state was the ninth to ratify, making the Constitution take effect?
questions.explain: New Hampshire ratified on June 21, 1788.
questions.tip: New Hampshire made nine: Live Free or Die.

questions.q: Which state was the first to ratify the Constitution?
questions.explain: Delaware ratified on December 7, 1787, earning the nickname the First State.
questions.tip: Delaware: the First State, on its license plates.

questions.q: Who presided over the Constitutional Convention?
questions.explain: Washington was unanimously chosen president of the Convention.
questions.tip: Washington chaired the Convention.

questions.q: Which compromise created a House based on population and a Senate with equal representation?
questions.explain: Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth of Connecticut proposed it.
questions.tip: The Great Compromise: big states and small states both win.

questions.q: The Virginia Plan favored representation based on population. What did the New Jersey Plan favor?
questions.explain: The Great Compromise blended the two plans.
questions.tip: Virginia was big; New Jersey was small.

questions.q: Which 1786-1787 uprising in Massachusetts exposed the weakness of the Articles of Confederation?
questions.explain: Shays' Rebellion helped build support for a stronger national government.
questions.tip: Shays' Rebellion shook the Articles.

questions.q: Who first proposed the amendments that became the Bill of Rights in the First Congress?
questions.explain: Madison introduced them in the House in 1789.
questions.tip: Madison: Father of the Constitution AND the Bill of Rights.

questions.q: Why did the colonists fight the British?
choices: High taxes without representation, soldiers housed in their homes, and lack of self-government
To gain more land in Europe
questions.explain: These are the reasons USCIS accepts.
questions.tip: No taxation without representation.

questions.q: What problem was a central cause of the Civil War?
questions.explain: USCIS accepts slavery, economic reasons and states' rights.
questions.tip: Slavery split the nation.
